section.title: The Outpouring of the Spirit
section.sectionRationale: This is the mountaintop of Joel and one of the great promises of the Old Testament. Beyond the restoration of crops lies a greater gift: God will pour out His Spirit on all people, without distinction of age, gender, or status. Peter stands up on the day of Pentecost and declares, this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel, making these five verses a hinge between the Testaments.
section.thesis: After restoring His people, God promises to pour out His Spirit on all flesh, so that in the last days, amid cosmic signs and the coming Day of the LORD, everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the promised outpouring of the Spirit on all people; the cosmic wonders before the great Day; and the sweeping promise that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved.

units.label: I will pour out My Spirit on all people
units.note: sons and daughters, old and young, servants

verses.text: And afterward, I will pour out My {{ruach|Spirit}} on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions.
Even on My menservants and maidservants, I will pour out My Spirit in those days.

units.label: Wonders before the great Day
units.note: the sun darkened, the moon to blood

verses.text: I will show wonders in the heavens and on the earth, blood and fire and columns of smoke.
The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the coming of the great and awesome {{yomYHWH|Day of the LORD}}.

units.label: Everyone who calls will be saved

verses.text: And everyone who {{qara|calls}} on the name of the LORD will be saved; for on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be deliverance, as the LORD has promised, among the remnant called by the LORD.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, breath, or wind. It is the same word for the Spirit of God who hovered over the waters at creation and empowered prophets, judges, and kings. In the old covenant the Spirit came upon select individuals for particular tasks; here God promises to pour Him out on all people, sons and daughters, old and young, servants alike, a democratizing of the Spirit fulfilled at Pentecost.

yomYHWH.gloss: The Day of the LORD, Joel's central theme, here called great and awesome. The outpouring of the Spirit and the cosmic signs belong to the last days that lead up to this Day. For those who call on the LORD it is a day of deliverance; for those who refuse, a day of reckoning. The New Testament sees these last days inaugurated at Pentecost and consummated at Christ's return.

qara.gloss: To call, to call out, to invoke by name. To call on the name of the LORD is to appeal to Him in trust for salvation, casting oneself on His mercy. Joel's promise is strikingly wide, everyone who calls will be saved, and Paul quotes it to show that this salvation is open to Jew and Gentile alike, Romans 10:13.

basic.context: Having promised to restore the harvest, God now promises something far greater: to pour out His Spirit on all people, not just prophets and kings but sons and daughters, old and young, male and female, servants included. This comes with cosmic signs before the great Day of the LORD, and the sweeping promise that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved.
basic.hermeneutics: Peter quotes this passage on the day of Pentecost, Acts 2, and says, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel, so the New Testament tells us how to read it: the last days began when the Spirit was poured out on the church. The wonders and the great Day point to the whole span from Pentecost to Christ's return, and the offer of salvation to all who call is the heart of it.
basic.originalLanguages: God promises to pour out His ruach, His Spirit, the same word for the breath that gave life at creation, now given to all people. The signs lead up to the yom YHWH, the great and awesome Day of the LORD. And salvation comes to everyone who will qara, call on the name of the LORD, casting themselves on His mercy.
basic.typology: The Spirit poured out on all flesh fulfills Moses' longing that all the LORD's people would be prophets, Numbers 11:29. The remnant who call on the LORD and are saved points to the church gathered from every nation. And the Day of the LORD frames the whole, first inaugurated at the cross and Pentecost, then consummated when Christ returns.
basic.christ: Peter proclaims at Pentecost that the risen and exalted Jesus is the one who pours out the Spirit He promised, Acts 2:33, so this outpouring is the direct gift of the ascended Christ. And the name people call on to be saved, which Joel names as the LORD, Peter applies to Jesus, everyone who calls on the name of the Lord Jesus will be saved. Joel's promise becomes the gospel invitation itself.
basic.god: God is generous beyond the old boundaries, no longer giving His Spirit to a few but pouring Him out on all kinds of people, erasing distinctions of age, gender, and status. He is both the just Judge of the great Day and the Saviour who opens deliverance to everyone who calls. His deepest desire is to dwell in His people by His Spirit and to save all who turn to Him.
basic.crossReferences: Peter quotes this at Pentecost, Acts 2:16-21. Paul quotes verse 32 in Romans 10:13, everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. Ezekiel 36 and Numbers 11 anticipate the Spirit poured out on all God's people.
basic.oneStory: This promise is the bridge from the old covenant to the new: the God who once gave His Spirit to a few now pours Him out on all who call. Fulfilled at Pentecost by the risen Christ, it opens the age of the Spirit and the worldwide invitation that runs to the ends of the earth and to the last Day.

context.literary:
Everything in this short unit turns on how it is hinged to the one before. The hinge is the opening word, 'afterward,' and the verses that follow are carried by repeated 'all' and 'everyone' language. 'All people' in verse 28, 'even on' the servants in verse 29, 'everyone who calls' in verse 32. Each of the three waves widens the door a little further. First the Spirit is given across age and sex, then across social rank, and finally the offer of rescue reaches anyone at all who calls.

The passage has a clear shape in three small panels. Verses 28 and 29 are a promise of the Spirit, written in a parallel pair of sentences, with the second adding the servants as a surprise. Verses 30 and 31 are a warning of cosmic upheaval, and they are bracketed by the word 'wonders' at the start and the 'great and awesome Day' at the end. Verse 32 is the resolution, a sentence of rescue that ends with a double use of the verb 'call': those who call on the LORD, and those whom the LORD calls. Notice that the middle panel is the only one with any terror in it, and it is wrapped on both sides by gift and rescue.

A small point about numbering helps readers. In the Hebrew Bible these five verses are chapter 3, verses 1 to 5, and what English Bibles call chapter 3 is chapter 4 of the Hebrew. The break in the English versions follows the logic of the passage, but the Hebrew division is a reminder that the outpouring is a hinge between the restoration speech and the final judgment of the nations. It looks back at the 'then you will know' of 2:27 and forward at the 'then you will know' of 3:17.

The gifts named are all forms of revelation: prophecy, dreams and visions. The Spirit does not arrive as an anonymous force but as the one who makes God known. That is why verse 28 lists speaking and seeing, and why the shape of the promise is not material wealth but nearness to God's voice.
context.historical:
For Joel's hearers, the gift of the Spirit was usually thought of as the equipment for a task. It came on judges such as Othniel and Gideon, Judges 3:10 and 6:34, on kings such as Saul and David, 1 Samuel 10:6 and 16:13, on craftsmen like Bezalel, Exodus 31:3, and on prophets. It could come and go. Prophecy was a recognised office held by a few, and Moses' own cry in Numbers 11:29, 'I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets,' voiced a longing that was clearly not the present situation. Joel's promise says that the longing will be answered, and that it will be answered widely.

The social range of the list is the surprising feature. Sons and daughters, old men and young men, men and women servants: the ancient world was graded by age, sex and rank, and the groups named here include those with the least public voice, the young, women and slaves. Joel does not say that these distinctions will vanish from society, but he does say that nearness to God's Spirit will not run along them. The servants in particular are told that the Spirit will fall on them, a reversal of the usual assumption that God's word comes through those with standing.

Dreams and visions were recognised channels of revelation. Numbers 12:6 says that the LORD makes Himself known to a prophet in a vision and speaks in a dream, and Joel's list reuses the language. In the ancient Near East dream interpretation was a specialist craft, and the royal courts of the time employed experts. The idea that dreams would come to ordinary old men was an unsettling one.

The 'wonders' of verses 30 and 31 draw on the vocabulary of the exodus, where the LORD's wonders in Egypt included blood and darkness, Exodus 7:3 and 10:21 to 23, and on the plainer language of the Day of the LORD in other prophets, Isaiah 13:10, Ezekiel 32:7 to 8 and Amos 8:9. Joel is not inventing the imagery. He is placing it in a sequence the audience already knew, which is why the final verse speaks of Zion and 'those who escape,' as Obadiah 17 does.
context.canonical:
This is one of the most consequential short passages in the Old Testament for the New. Peter quotes it at length on the day of Pentecost, Acts 2:17 to 21, and introduces the quotation with the claim 'this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel.' Paul quotes the last line in Romans 10:13 to establish that salvation is for everyone who calls on the Lord, Jew or Greek, Romans 10:12. The BSB footnote at Joel 2:32 notes both citations.

Behind it stands a series of promises that the Spirit would one day be poured out on the whole people. Numbers 11:29 is Moses' wish. Isaiah 32:15 foresees the Spirit poured out from on high, so that the wilderness becomes a fruitful field. Isaiah 44:3 pairs water on thirsty ground with the Spirit on descendants. Ezekiel 36:26 to 27 promises a new heart and God's own Spirit within, and Ezekiel 39:29 uses the same verb as Joel, pour out, when God says He will pour out His Spirit on the house of Israel. Zechariah 12:10 speaks of a spirit of grace and prayer poured out on Jerusalem. Joel is the one who says it will be on 'all flesh,' and who sets it before the final Day.

The theme of calling on the name of the LORD is rooted in the earliest chapters of the Bible. Genesis 4:26 notes that in the days of Enosh men began to call on the name of the LORD, Abram called on the name of the LORD, Genesis 12:8, and the psalmist promises to do so in thanks for rescue, Psalm 116:13. Zephaniah 3:9 and Zechariah 13:9 look forward to a purified people who do so. The New Testament carries the line into the church: Paul addresses those who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, 1 Corinthians 1:2.

The cosmic signs reappear in the Gospels, in Jesus' account of the end, Matthew 24:29, in the darkness at the crucifixion, Luke 23:44 to 45, and in the sixth seal of Revelation, Revelation 6:12, where the sun turns black and the moon turns the colour of blood. Joel's passage therefore sits at the crossing of three great themes: the Spirit, the Day and the offer of salvation.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Joel was telling a chastened and hopeful community that the best was still ahead. The restoration of crops was real and welcome, but the word 'afterward' sets a further and larger gift beyond it. He wanted them to hold two things together: that God's relation to His people would one day be closer than it had ever been, and that this closeness would be shared, not reserved for a few leaders. The long frustration of Moses, who wished that all the LORD's people were prophets, was going to be met.

He also meant to place the gift inside the frame of the coming Day. The Spirit is not offered as a comfortable add-on to ordinary life but as the way God prepares a people for the great and awesome Day. This is why the promise and the warning stand side by side. The hearers are being asked to see that the same God who pours out His Spirit will also shake the heavens, and that the only safe place on that Day is in the company of those who call on the name of the LORD.

The last verse carries the pastoral purpose of the whole unit. Joel does not leave his hearers with a spectacle. He closes by handing them an action, to call, and a promise, to be saved. The universal language, 'everyone,' is a deliberate answer to anyone who thought that rescue was a matter of status or merit. Whoever calls, in whatever condition, is to find a door open.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage is a promise and a prophecy, so it describes what God will do rather than commanding what people must do. The only implied command is in the final verse: to call on the name of the LORD. The rest tells believers what to expect and what to hope for. It is not a programme to be manufactured by human effort. People cannot arrange for their sons and daughters to prophesy or for their old men to dream, and the passage does not ask them to.

It is also not a detailed list of what every Christian must experience. Peter's use of the passage shows that the entire pattern, prophecy, visions, dreams, is a description of the age that opens with the Spirit's coming, and the New Testament treats the Spirit's presence, not each particular phenomenon, as the point. Paul can say that in one Spirit all believers were baptised into one body and given one Spirit to drink, 1 Corinthians 12:13, and that no one belongs to Christ without Him, Romans 8:9.

What the passage does require of readers is a hopeful and humble stance. They should expect the Spirit to be given widely, without regard to age, sex or social standing, and so should refuse to treat any believer's voice as less important in the church on those grounds. Galatians 3:28 draws the same implication. They should take the offer in verse 32 as an open door, and call. And they should treat the language about the signs and the Day as a sober backdrop that makes the gift of the Spirit and the offer of rescue more precious, not as material for speculation about dates.

debates.question: How does Pentecost relate to Joel's promise, and what of the cosmic signs?

views.label: Fulfilled at Pentecost and in the whole church age
views.case: Peter's words, 'this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel,' Acts 2:16, and his change of 'afterward' to 'in the last days,' Acts 2:17, treat the whole period from Pentecost onward as the age Joel foresaw. The sun's darkness and the blood-red moon are read as imagery of the Day of the LORD, with the darkness at the cross, Luke 23:44 to 45, as a pointer, and the entire age as the time in which 'everyone who calls' may be saved.

views.label: Begun at Pentecost, completed at the return of Christ
views.case: The signs of verses 30 and 31 are tied to 'the coming of the great and awesome Day,' and the New Testament still looks forward to that Day, Matthew 24:29 to 31 and Revelation 6:12. On this view Pentecost is the first stage of a fulfilment that is not complete until the Lord returns, which is why Acts 2:19 to 20 can quote all of it in one breath.

views.label: Only a typological parallel, with fulfilment in Israel's future
views.case: Some argue that Peter says only that this is like what Joel foretold, and that the promise to Israel of a national outpouring awaits its own time. Others reply that Peter's plain wording, 'this is what,' leaves little room for that.

debates.bearing: Most readers across the Christian tradition accept an inaugurated fulfilment: the Spirit has been poured out and the last days have begun, but the Day and its signs are not over. The passage invites believers to live in that overlap.

debates.question: How wide is 'all flesh' in verse 28?

views.label: All of God's covenant people, without distinction of age, sex or rank
views.case: The list that follows, sons, daughters, old, young, servants, shows that the 'all' is described by categories within Israel. On this reading Joel's emphasis is that every kind of member of the people will receive the Spirit.

views.label: Every nation, Jew and Gentile
views.case: The Hebrew phrase 'all flesh' elsewhere has an unbounded sense, Isaiah 40:5, and the end of the passage opens the invitation to 'everyone.' Peter says the promise is for 'all who are far off,' Acts 2:39, and the Gentile household of Cornelius receives the Spirit poured out, Acts 10:45. Paul presses the same point, Romans 10:12.

debates.bearing: The two readings are not rivals. The immediate sense is the breadth within Israel, and the New Testament shows God extending the same promise beyond Israel without altering its terms. The movement is from a surprising breadth to an unlimited one.

debates.question: Do prophecy, dreams and visions continue in the church today?

views.label: Yes, the pattern of Pentecost continues
views.case: Because the age that began at Pentecost is the age of the outpouring, Peter's 'all who are far off' and the promise of verse 28 are taken to cover all later believers. Gifts of prophecy are described in 1 Corinthians 12 to 14 as normal in the churches, to be tested and valued.

views.label: No, the foundational gifts served the apostolic age
views.case: Others argue that the revelatory gifts accompanied the founding of the church and that Scripture is now complete, Hebrews 1:1 to 2 and Jude 3. On this view the lasting content of Joel's promise is the Spirit's indwelling and illumination of all believers, not new revelation.

debates.bearing: Believers who differ on this still share the central claim: the Spirit is given to every believer who belongs to Christ, and every voice in the body matters. The disagreement is about particular gifts, not about the generosity of the promise.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb 'pour out' is shaphakh, and it is a physical word. It is used for pouring water, Isaiah 44:3 uses a related image, and for the shedding of blood, as in Genesis 9:6, and Scripture uses it for pouring out wrath, Ezekiel 36:18. Joel uses it for the Spirit, and so does Ezekiel 39:29 and Zechariah 12:10. The picture is not of a trickle or a loan but of a liquid emptied freely from a vessel. In Acts 2:17 and 2:33 the Greek equivalent is ekcheo, and Titus 3:6 uses it again when Paul says that the Spirit was poured out on believers abundantly through Jesus Christ.

The 'all flesh' of verse 28, kol basar, is the Bible's phrase for living humanity in its frailty. It was the phrase for the generation of the flood, Genesis 6:12, and it describes all who will see the glory of the LORD in Isaiah 40:5. In Joel it is set beside a list of the sorts of people who will receive the Spirit, so the phrase works in two directions: it names ordinary, mortal human beings as the recipients of the Spirit of God. The Spirit, ruach, is in Hebrew breath, wind and spirit all at once, which is why Ezekiel 37 can pass so easily between breath entering the bones and the Spirit entering the people, Ezekiel 37:9 to 10 and 37:14.

Verse 29 begins with 'even,' gam, a small particle with a large effect. After saying that sons and daughters, old men and young men would receive the Spirit, God adds, 'even on the servants.' The word is a reminder that the list is not exhausted by the categories one would have expected. The servants are male and female, avadim and shefachot, the slaves and maidservants who were the lowest rank of a household.

The 'wonders' of verse 30 are mofetim, the term used of the exodus miracles in Exodus 7:3 and of signs that confirm a prophet in Deuteronomy 13:1 to 2. Peter's quotation in Acts 2:19 adds the word 'signs,' semeia, and places 'above' and 'below' around heavens and earth. He then uses the same pairing for Jesus' own ministry, 'miracles, wonders and signs,' Acts 2:22, which ties the two together. The BSB's footnote at Joel 2:30 notes that the Septuagint reads 'clouds or billows' for the columns of smoke, which is the form Peter quotes.

The phrase 'great and awesome' in verse 31 uses a word, nora, from the root of fear and reverence. The same adjective appears in Malachi 4:5 in its description of the Day. The BSB footnote notes that the same word can be read 'dreadful,' and that the Septuagint reads 'glorious,' which is the form quoted in Acts 2:20. The two translations show how the same event looks different to those who face it with and without the LORD.

The final verse turns on the verb qara, 'to call,' and on the way it occurs twice. 'Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD' uses the verb for human petition and proclamation, and the clause 'the remnant called by the LORD' uses the same verb for His summons. The human calling is thus matched by a divine calling. Peter ends his sermon on this note when he says that the promise belongs to all 'whom the Lord our God will call to Himself,' Acts 2:39. The word for 'deliverance,' peletah, comes from the root for slipping away, escaping, and appears in Obadiah 17 with the same Mount Zion setting. And the word 'saved' is a form of malat, 'to escape,' which is the verb used when the angels told Lot to flee for his life in Genesis 19:17. Rescue in Joel is the language of escape from a coming disaster.

typology.type: Moses' longing and the seventy elders, Numbers 11:25-29
typology.fulfillment: When the Spirit rested on seventy elders and on Eldad and Medad in the camp, Moses answered the complaint with a wish that all the LORD's people were prophets. The scene is a small picture of a gift spreading beyond the usual channel. Joel announces that the wish will come true, and Acts 2 records the day on which the Spirit rests on a whole company of men and women at once, Acts 2:1 to 4. The escalation is from seventy to all flesh, and from a temporary resting to a permanent indwelling, John 14:16 to 17. The type falls short because the elders prophesied and did not continue, Numbers 11:25.

typology.type: The Spirit poured out like water on dry ground
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 44:3 links water on thirsty land with the Spirit on descendants, and Joel's rains of chapter 2 lead directly into this pouring out. Jesus uses the same imagery on the last day of the feast, inviting the thirsty to come and drink and promising streams of living water from within, which John explains as the Spirit, John 7:37 to 39. The pouring in Acts 2:33 is attributed to Christ. The type is partial in that rain reaches a field from outside, but the Spirit is given to dwell within believers, Romans 8:9.

typology.type: The breath over the valley of bones
typology.fulfillment: The Hebrew ruach is breath as well as Spirit, and Ezekiel 37 pictures the breath entering slain bodies so that they stand as a vast army. Ezekiel then explains that God will put His Spirit within the people and they will live, Ezekiel 37:14. Joel's outpouring belongs to the same picture of new life given by the Spirit. At Pentecost the sound like a rushing wind, Acts 2:2, recalls it, and in John 20:22 the risen Jesus breathes on the disciples and says, Receive the Holy Spirit. The type is incomplete because the valley's life belongs to a nation, while the church's belongs to people from every nation.

typology.type: The remnant on Mount Zion who escape
typology.fulfillment: Joel's last verse sets rescue on Mount Zion among those called by the LORD. Obadiah 17 shares the setting. The New Testament says believers have come to Mount Zion, to the heavenly Jerusalem, Hebrews 12:22 to 24, and that they are gathered from every tribe and language, Revelation 7:9. The fulfilment widens the remnant from a surviving community in Judah to a people from all nations, and from escape in a city to rescue by the blood of Christ. The type is partial as long as that city is still approached by faith rather than by sight.

study.christ:
This passage leads to Christ with unusual directness, because the apostle Peter tells us how. On the day of Pentecost he explains the sound of wind and the tongues of fire as the fulfillment of Joel, and then he describes where the Spirit came from. Jesus, he says, was raised up and exalted to the right hand of God, and He 'has received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and has poured out what you now see and hear,' Acts 2:33. The verb 'pour out' is Joel's verb. In Joel, God says, 'I will pour out My Spirit.' In Peter's account, the one who pours out is the risen Jesus. The sentence assigns to the Son the action that Joel assigns to the LORD, and it does so without any sense of strain.

It leads to Christ again by the name that saves. Joel says that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved, and the LORD in this verse is the covenant name, Yahweh. Peter ends his quotation of the verse in Acts 2:21 and then turns immediately to Jesus, whom God has made both Lord and Christ, Acts 2:36. Paul reads the verse the same way. In Romans 10:9 to 13 he moves from the confession that Jesus is Lord to the quotation of Joel 2:32 in one connected argument, so that the Lord on whose name people call is Jesus. The first Christians were known as those who call on the name, Acts 9:14, and Paul writes to those who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, 1 Corinthians 1:2. A prophetic line about calling on Yahweh becomes the gospel invitation to call on Jesus.

It leads to Christ by the preparation for the Day. The cosmic signs, the darkened sun and the blood-red moon, may be echoed when darkness covered the land at midday on the day of the crucifixion, Luke 23:44 to 45, though the Gospels do not quote Joel there. Peter says that Joel's signs and Jesus' own 'miracles, wonders and signs,' Acts 2:22, belong together. The cross is the place where the judgment of the Day was borne for those who call.

It leads to Christ by the shape of the gift. Joel puts the Spirit on all kinds of people, and Paul says that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, Galatians 3:28. The Spirit's generosity across categories is what the cross made possible, for the middle wall was broken down, Ephesians 2:14 to 18.

A note of restraint. Joel himself does not name the Messiah in this passage, and no honest reading would say he does. What he gives is a promise of the Spirit and a promise of rescue for those who call, and the New Testament shows that both are carried by Christ. The link rests on Peter's and Paul's own use of the text, and it is strong enough to need no more.
study.god:
The passage presents a God who gives Himself. The gift of verse 28 is not rain or grain but 'My Spirit,' and the promise is that He will pour out His own breath on people. The one who gives is the same as the gift. This is a bold thing to say about a holy God, and it shows that holiness in the Bible does not mean distance. The holy One closes the distance by coming to His people in His Spirit.

He is generous beyond the boundaries people draw. The list of recipients keeps widening, young and old, male and female, free and servant, until the final word is 'everyone.' God's love of order did not stop Him from giving to the lowliest, and the promise to servants is the plainest sign of that. A God who gave the Spirit only to those with standing would be a God with a limited reach. Joel's God is not that.

He is a God who reveals. The gifts named, prophecy, dreams and visions, are all about hearing and seeing God. He wants to be known, and the age of the Spirit is an age in which His voice is not rationed. This links to the end of the previous unit, where the goal of the restoration was that the people would know Him, 2:27.

He is the Lord of history and the one who shakes the heavens. The signs of verses 30 and 31 belong to the same God who pours out His Spirit. The unit holds mercy and terror in a single sentence, and it does not apologise for either. The Day is 'great and awesome,' and the God who brings it is the God who opens the way of escape. The two belong together, because His mercy would be trivial if there were nothing to be rescued from.

He is a God who can be called upon. The whole structure of verse 32 rests on the fact that the God who is high and holy can be reached by anyone who cries to Him. No priest or qualification stands between the caller and the LORD. And He is the God who calls first: the 'remnant called by the LORD' shows that human calling is a response to a prior summons. Salvation is therefore both open to all and securely God's own work.

He is faithful to His purposes. The longing of Moses in Numbers 11:29, the promises of Isaiah and Ezekiel, and the pouring out in Joel form one line of intention that the LORD carries through. For worship this means that confidence is appropriate. We are not guessing at a God who might give His Spirit; we are responding to one who said He would and then did.

crossReferences.note: Peter explains the sound of the Spirit's coming by quoting Joel 2:28 to 32. He changes 'afterward' to 'in the last days,' adds 'signs' and the phrase 'and they will prophesy,' and follows the Greek Old Testament's wording in places. The citation shows that the apostles read Joel's promise as having begun with the gift of the Spirit to the church.

The Spirit rests on seventy elders and on two men in the camp, and Moses answers a complaint with the wish that all the LORD's people were prophets. The longing for a Spirit-filled people is already in the Torah, and Joel is the prophet who says it will be granted.

God promises to replace the heart of stone with a heart of flesh and to put His Spirit within His people so that they walk in His ways. Joel describes the Spirit poured out, and Ezekiel describes what the Spirit does within, which together give a fuller account of the new covenant gift.

The same verb as Joel's, pour out, is used when God promises to pour out His Spirit on the house of Israel and never again hide His face. It shows that the outpouring is tied to the end of exile and to the permanent presence of God with His people, a theme that Joel shares.

God speaks to Jacob His servant and promises to pour water on thirsty land and His Spirit on their descendants, so that they spring up like willows by streams. The image of water and Spirit as one gift stands behind Joel's rains of chapter 2 flowing straight into the outpouring in verse 28.

God promises to pour out a spirit of grace and prayer on Jerusalem, and the people look on the One they pierced and mourn for Him. The passage joins the pouring out of the Spirit to repentance and to the pierced One, whom John 19:37 identifies with Jesus on the cross.

Paul confesses that Jesus is Lord and then quotes Joel 2:32, 'Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved,' to show that there is no difference between Jew and Greek. The apostle thereby reads the name of the LORD in Joel as the name of the Lord Jesus.

After quoting Joel, Peter says that the promise is for his hearers, their children and all who are far off, all whom the Lord will call. The words 'call' and 'far off' reflect the language of Joel's final verse and make plain that the offer reaches beyond the audience that day.

The Spirit falls on Gentiles in the household of Cornelius while Peter is still speaking, and the Jewish believers are astounded that the gift was poured out even on the Gentiles. The event shows that Joel's 'all flesh' reaches beyond Israel in the way the final verse anticipated.

God promises to send Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD, in the same words Joel uses for the Day. The two prophets together show that the Day has a herald, and the New Testament connects the herald to John the Baptist, Matthew 11:14.

Paul says that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, and that believers are Abraham's offspring and heirs. The categories that Joel lists as receiving the Spirit without distinction are here described as one in Christ, and the promise of the Spirit appears in the same chapter, Galatians 3:14.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with God breathing into the first man and the man becoming a living being, Genesis 2:7. The word for breath and Spirit is the same word that Joel uses here. The fall broke that nearness, and the story from then on is a long search for the way in which the breath of God will once again fill the whole human family. Joel's promise sits at a crucial point on that road. It states that the Spirit will not be rationed to a few special people but poured out on all flesh, and it names the day on which that reversal begins.

What the passage answers from earlier in the story is the question raised by Moses in Numbers 11:29. The wilderness generation had seen that a few were given the Spirit, and it had seen how limited that was. The same longing is in the prophets who spoke of a new heart and a new spirit, Ezekiel 36:26 to 27, and of the Spirit poured out from on high, Isaiah 32:15. Joel adds that the gift will not be limited by age, sex or rank, and that it will arrive in the shadow of the Day of the LORD.

What the passage sets up is the age of the church. Pentecost is the day on which the exalted Christ pours out the Spirit, Acts 2:33, and the breadth that Joel promised becomes visible on the street in Jerusalem, in many languages, from many nations. The story then moves outward in Acts, from Jerusalem to Samaria to the ends of the earth, as the Spirit falls on groups that Joel's original hearers would not have expected, Acts 8 and Acts 10. The offer in verse 32 is the engine of that mission. Everyone who calls will be saved, so the news must be carried to those who have not yet heard, Romans 10:14 to 15.

It also sets up the end. The cosmic signs and the great Day that frame the promise are not left behind by Pentecost. They await the return of Christ, as the Gospels and Revelation describe, Matthew 24:29 to 31 and Revelation 6:12 to 17. The gift of the Spirit is described in the New Testament as the guarantee and first instalment of what is to come, Ephesians 1:13 to 14. The church lives between the outpouring and the Day, with the Spirit as the pledge that the rest will come.

In the new creation the promise is complete. The Spirit and the bride say 'Come,' and whoever is thirsty is invited to take the water of life, Revelation 22:17. The stream that Joel saw flowing from the house of the LORD in the last chapter, 3:18, becomes the river flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 22:1. The breath that God breathed into the first man fills a redeemed creation, and everyone who called on the name of the LORD is gathered into the city where God dwells with them.

quiz.q: What is new and striking about the outpouring of the Spirit Joel promises?

options.text: The Spirit is poured out on all kinds of people, regardless of age, gender, or status.
options.note: Sons and daughters, old and young, male and female servants all receive the Spirit.

options.text: The Spirit will finally come upon a few chosen prophets.
options.note: That was the old-covenant pattern; the new thing is the Spirit on all people.

options.text: The Spirit is given more widely than ever before, to ordinary believers of every kind.
options.note: True, and specifically without the old distinctions of age, gender, and status.

options.text: The Spirit is given only to those who earn Him by good works.
options.note: The Spirit is poured out as a gift, not earned.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament say this passage is fulfilled?

options.text: Peter declares at Pentecost, 'this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel.'
options.note: Acts 2 identifies Pentecost as the fulfillment of Joel's promise.

options.text: It is treated as still entirely future, with no fulfillment yet begun.
options.note: Peter says it began at Pentecost, though its consummation awaits Christ's return.

options.text: It is quoted to show the gospel goes out to all nations.
options.note: True, especially in Romans 10, though the primary fulfillment marker is Pentecost.

options.text: It is never referred to again in the New Testament.
options.note: It is quoted at length in Acts 2 and again in Romans 10.

quiz.q: Who pours out the Spirit, according to Peter at Pentecost?

options.text: The risen and exalted Jesus, who received the promised Spirit from the Father.
options.note: Acts 2:33 makes the ascended Christ the giver of the Spirit.

options.text: The apostles, by their own authority.
options.note: The Spirit is poured out by Christ, not by the apostles' own power.

options.text: God the Father alone, apart from Christ.
options.note: The Father gives through the exalted Son, who pours out the Spirit.

options.text: God, through the exalted Christ who now reigns.
options.note: True, and Peter specifies it is Jesus who has poured out what was seen and heard.

quiz.q: What does 'everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved' mean in its New Testament use?

options.text: Salvation is open to all, Jew and Gentile, who call on the Lord Jesus in trust.
options.note: Paul quotes this in Romans 10:13 to ground the worldwide gospel offer.

options.text: Only Israel may call on the LORD and be saved.
options.note: Paul uses the verse precisely to show the offer extends to all nations.

options.text: Anyone who sincerely turns to God for rescue will be received.
options.note: True, and the New Testament specifies that name as the Lord Jesus.

options.text: Salvation comes automatically to everyone without any response.
options.note: The promise is to those who call, an act of trust, not automatic to all.

quiz.q: How do the cosmic signs and the 'great and awesome Day' fit the timeline?

options.text: Pentecost begins the last days, while the great Day and its signs await Christ's return.
options.note: The New Testament holds an 'already and not yet': the Spirit is given, the Day is still coming.

options.text: They were all completely fulfilled on the day of Pentecost with nothing left.
options.note: The outpouring began, but the great Day and its cosmic signs are still future.

options.text: They point to a fullness still to come at the end of the age.
options.note: True of the great Day, while the Spirit's outpouring has already begun.

options.text: They are purely symbolic and refer to no real future events.
options.note: Scripture treats the coming Day as real, both promised and awaited.

questions: Joel promised the Spirit for sons and daughters, old and young, servants and all. How does it change your sense of your own place before God to know His Spirit is poured out on ordinary believers like you?
The passage ends with 'everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved.' Have you called on Him yourself? What holds you back from casting yourself fully on His mercy?
Peter says the risen Jesus is the one who pours out the Spirit. How does living in the age of the Spirit shape the way you pray, serve, and expect God to work?
The promise erases old distinctions of status and gender in access to God. How should that shape the way your church values and includes every kind of person?
The great and awesome Day is still coming. How does holding both the gift of the Spirit and the certainty of that Day together help you live with urgency and hope?

translationNotes.note: 'On all people' renders the Hebrew 'on all flesh'; in Hebrew Bibles these verses are numbered 3:1-5, while English versions place them at the end of chapter 2.
BSB footnotes that the Septuagint reads 'clouds' or 'billows' where the Hebrew has 'columns' of smoke; the imagery of upheaval is unchanged.
'Great and awesome' translates the Hebrew; BSB notes an alternative 'dreadful,' and the Septuagint reads 'glorious.' The Day is both fearsome to enemies and glorious for the saved.
BSB notes this verse is cited in Acts 2:17-21 and Romans 10:13, both applying it to salvation through the Lord Jesus.
